title: Lesson 74 - If We Hadn't Been So Busy…

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Now that we’ve read everything, I can see the chain. If I hadn’t replied before talking to you, you wouldn’t feel that your choice had been taken away now.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yes. And if Carla hadn’t turned “don’t count on her” into “Maya won’t be joining,” the group wouldn’t currently have a final answer that I never gave.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: That’s a fair point; however, I wrote the phrase that made that summary possible. I can’t treat her wording as the whole cause.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I agree that several steps mattered. Even so, your reply is the step we can address inside our relationship.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: If I were less quick to solve problems for people, I might have forwarded the invitation instead of deciding what would reduce pressure.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That feels more precise. It explains how a present habit affected one past action, but I don’t want us to turn your whole personality into the problem.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Then I’d put it more narrowly: if I weren’t so used to responding immediately, I might have paused on this message.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That sounds fair. I have a pattern too. If I hadn’t said yes to so many requests recently, you might not have been as worried about sending me another one.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Maybe, but that doesn’t make my choice your fault. At the time, I knew you felt overloaded; I did not know that you wanted every request forwarded unchanged.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And you didn’t ask. Looking back, I can see that I had complained about pressure without explaining the boundary I actually wanted.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: A possible objection is that we’re building a perfect solution with information we only have now. What could we reasonably have done then?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You could have sent one line: “Carla asked about Thursday; do you want the message now or tomorrow?” That would have protected both rest and choice.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I may not have thought of that exact wording, but I could have avoided answering about your availability. That option was available to me at the time.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: For my part, I could have said, “Please reduce reminders, but don’t answer invitations for me.” I had enough information to state that earlier.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: The evidence still supports a shared condition: we were both moving too quickly because the week was crowded.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I would qualify that by saying the pressure was shared, while the actions were separate. Busy schedules did not send the reply; you did, and my vague boundary did not help.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Overall, the most defensible conclusion is not “If we hadn’t been busy, none of this would have happened.” We can’t know that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. A better conclusion is that time pressure made our existing habits more likely to shape the exchange.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: If we change those habits now, this misunderstanding won’t have to become our normal way of handling requests.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then the useful question is not who caused everything. It is which past choice still affects us now, which present habit influenced it and what we will do differently next time.
